explainers.title: Why your equation is 'wrong' even when it's right
explainers.hook: You wrote Mg + O2 -> MgO in the exam. Correct reaction, na? Still zero. The examiner's red pen didn't even blink.
explainers.concept: Atoms can't appear or vanish mid-reaction - that's the law of conservation of mass (NCERT Ch.1, §1.1.2). Mg + O2 -> MgO has 2 oxygens entering and only 1 leaving. An unbalanced equation claims matter vanished, so it's not an approximation, it's wrong. Balance with coefficients only: 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO. Never touch the formula itself.
explainers.hack: Write the unbalanced equation first, then balance it as a separate visible step. Examiners award the balancing mark when they SEE the step. Doing it in your head hides your own mark.
explainers.hackSource: Visible step-by-step answers work like self-explanation - Make It Stick (Brown, Roediger & McDaniel, 2014).

explainers.title: The 4 reaction types are 4 dance moves
explainers.hook: Combination = two people become one couple. Decomposition = couple splits, both dance solo. Displacement = someone cuts in. Double displacement = everyone swaps partners.
explainers.concept: NCERT Ch.1 defines them by pattern: A+B->AB (combination, Eq. 1.13), AB->A+B (decomposition, Eq. 1.19-1.22), A+BC->AC+B (displacement, Activity 1.9), AB+CD->AD+CB (double displacement, Activity 1.10). Identify the PATTERN first, name the reaction second - never the other way round.
explainers.hack: Before the exam, take 10 random equations and sort them into the 4 patterns out loud. Sorting mixed types beats studying one type at a time - that's interleaving.
explainers.hackSource: Interleaving mixed practice improves discrimination between problem types - Make It Stick (Brown, Roediger & McDaniel, 2014).

explainers.title: Your body's heating bill: exo vs endo
explainers.hook: Ever touched a beaker when quicklime met water in the lab? It burns. That beaker was paying out heat like a heater with the window open.
explainers.concept: Exothermic = heat released along with products (NCERT Ch.1, after Eq. 1.17): burning, respiration (Eq. 1.18: glucose + oxygen -> CO2 + water + energy), CaO + water. Endothermic = heat absorbed: thermal decomposition of CaCO3, photosynthesis. Respiration is the classic trap - it FEELS like nothing is burning, but it releases energy, so it's exothermic.
explainers.hack: When a 'which is exothermic?' MCQ appears, physically recall the warm-beaker feeling for 5 seconds, then answer. Tying facts to a sensory memory makes them stickier.
explainers.hackSource: Linking new facts to concrete memories aids retrieval - Make It Stick (2014); retrieval itself strengthens memory (Roediger & Karpicke, Psychological Science, 2006).

explainers.title: The brown powder eating your cycle
explainers.hook: That reddish-brown powder on an old cycle isn't dirt. It's the iron literally reacting away into the air, molecule by molecule.
explainers.concept: Corrosion: a metal is attacked by substances around it - moisture, acids (NCERT Ch.1, §1.3.1). Rusting is iron's corrosion; silver blackens and copper turns green too. Rancidity is the food version: fats and oils get oxidised, smell and taste change (§1.3.2). Prevention from the same chapter: antioxidants, airtight containers, nitrogen-flushed chip bags.
explainers.hack: Rancidity's three preventions come as a 2-marker nearly every cycle. Recite them from memory right now without looking - if you can't, that's the one to revise tonight.
explainers.hackSource: Self-testing beats re-reading for long-term retention - Roediger & Karpicke, Psychological Science (2006); spacing over days - Ebbinghaus (1885).

explainers.title: Water splits, but only if you add a pinch of chemistry
explainers.hook: A student connects a battery to plain distilled water. Nothing happens. Bulb stays dark. The exam asks WHY - and 'no electricity' is not the answer.
explainers.concept: Distilled water is a poor conductor; a few drops of dilute H2SO4 make it conduct (NCERT Ch.1, Activity 1.7). Then: 2H2O -> 2H2 + O2, hydrogen at the cathode at DOUBLE the volume of oxygen at the anode. This was CBSE Sample Paper 2025-26 Q27, all three parts.
explainers.hack: Remember 'cathode = H2 = double'. One anchor fact, and the anode answer falls out free. Anchor facts beat re-reading whole paragraphs.
explainers.hackSource: Small retrieval anchors strengthen recall of linked facts - Roediger & Karpicke (2006).

explainers.title: One breaks into many, three different ways
explainers.hook: Limestone in a kiln, water under current, a photograph fading in sunlight - three unrelated scenes, one reaction type.
explainers.concept: Decomposition = one reactant breaks into two or more products (NCERT Ch.1, Eq. 1.19-1.22). The three triggers: HEAT (thermal: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2; 2FeSO4 -> Fe2O3 + SO2 + SO3), ELECTRICITY (electrolytic: 2H2O -> 2H2 + O2), LIGHT (photolytic: 2AgCl -> 2Ag + Cl2, why photo films hate sunlight).
explainers.hack: Teach this to a friend (or our Junior) without notes. Explaining the three triggers with one example each is the fastest way to find out which one you actually don't know.
explainers.hackSource: Learning by teaching - Kobayashi meta-analysis (Japanese Psychological Research, 2019); the Feynman technique.
